turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: You are playing with fire, Sandip, and it is only a matter of time before your actions spark a blaze that will engulf us all.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Bimala, my dear, I see you're enjoying the show. Do tell Nikhil here that his warnings are as useless as his poetry.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: I think we should listen to Nikhil's concerns, Sandip. His words, though harsh, hold some truth.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: I have tried to warn you, Sandip, but it seems you are more concerned with your own interests than the well-being of this community.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: And what's the 'well-being of this community' to you, Nikhil? Is it not just a cover for your own power-hungry ambitions?

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: But what of the villagers, Nikhil? What of their well-being? Have you considered their perspective in all this?

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: I will not engage in frivolous banter, Sandip. The safety of our people is not a matter for jest or personal attacks.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: And yet, Nikhil, you're the one who's been stirring up trouble with your divisive rhetoric, not me.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: I have warned you before, Sandip, but it seems you will not heed the warning. The Mussulmans are growing restless and I fear for the safety of our people if action is not taken.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Oh, spare us the theatrics, Nikhil. If the Mussulmans are so 'restless', perhaps you should take a good look in the mirror and wonder if your own actions haven't contributed to this 'restlessness'.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: I have taken every precaution to ensure the safety of our people, and it is not for you to question my actions, Sandip. You would do well to focus on your own responsibilities rather than casting aspersions on mine.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: I'm not casting aspersions, Nikhil, I'm simply pointing out the obvious: you're more concerned with maintaining your own power than with the well-being of our people.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: I will not engage in a debate with you, Sandip. As a zamindar, it is my duty to protect our people, and I will not be swayed by your provocations.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Really, Nikhil, you're so quick to lecture others on their responsibilities, but how many times have you actually lifted a finger to improve the lives of our people?

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: I have done more for this community than you have, Sandip, and I will not be maligned by your petty insults.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: I have watched you both argue, and yet I have not heard any concrete plans for addressing the concerns you both raise.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Oh, Nikhil, always so quick to defend the honor of our people, but never so swift to actually do anything about it, unless it suits your own interests, of course.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Sandip, your flippant attitude is a threat to the stability of our community, and I will not stand idly by while you undermine the efforts of those who genuinely seek to improve our people's lives.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: And what exactly do you propose we do, Nikhil, to appease the Mussulmans? Play a game of 'good little zamindars' and beg for their mercy? I think not.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: I will not be lectured to by you, Sandip, on how to address the concerns of our people. I have concrete proposals for the militia and the distribution of our resources to ensure our community's safety and prosperity.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: I say, Nikhil, don't you keep Browning among your books here? I was just telling Queen Bee of our college club. Do you remember that contest of ours over the translation of those lines from Browning? You don't?

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: I managed to get together the words to render it into Bengali, somehow, but the result was hardly likely to be a 'joy forever' to the people of Bengal. I really did think at one time that I was on the verge of becoming a poet, but Providence was kind enough to save me from that disaster. Do you remember old Dakshina? If he had not become a Salt Inspector, he would have been a poet. I remember his rendering to this day ...

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: No, Queen Bee, it is no use rummaging those bookshelves. Nikhil has ceased to read poetry since his marriage--perhaps he has no further need for it. But I suppose 'the fever fit of poesy', as the Sanskrit has it, is about to attack me again.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: I have come to give you a warning, Sandip

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: About the fever fit of poesy?

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: For some time, Mahomedan preachers have been about stirring up the local Mussulmans. They are all wild with you, and may attack you any moment.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Are you come to advise flight?

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: I have come to give you information, not to offer advice.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Had these estates been mine, such a warning would have been necessary for the preachers, not for me. If, instead of trying to frighten me, you give them a taste of your intimidation, that would be worthier both of you and me. Do you know that your weakness is weakening your neighbouring zamindars also?

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: I did not offer you my advice, Sandip. I wish you, too, would refrain from giving me yours. Besides, it is useless. And there is another thing I want to tell you. You and your followers have been secretly worrying and oppressing my tenantry. I cannot allow that any longer. So I must ask you to leave my territory.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: For fear of the Mussulmans, or is there any other fear you have to threaten me with?
